141.title: Holika Dahan: the boy in the fire
141.hook: the night before the colors: a boy who wouldn't stop saying the name, and the fire that couldn't burn him
141.carry: bhakti: prahlada held the name, and it held him
141.howItsDone: On the full-moon night before Holi, many Hindu communities light a bonfire for Holika Dahan, retelling the story of Prahlada, walking around the fire, offering grain and coconut, and roasting new wheat or barley; the colors are played the next morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali ended: Lakshmi at the open door, a hill lifted over everyone, a sister's blessing. Your line was Krishna shelters everyone who comes under.

The famous photos of Holi show people drenched in pink and green and yellow powder, laughing in the street. But that's the morning. The night before, in towns and villages and temple courtyards, people gather around a great pile of wood and dried branches, sometimes with a figure set on top. At the right moment, it's lit, and the flames go up into the full-moon sky. People walk around it, throw in grain and coconuts, and hold up stalks of fresh wheat to roast. And somebody's grandmother tells the story, again, about a little boy who sat in a fire and walked out.
screen: `BEFORE THE COLORS, A BONFIRE.` → `THE FULL MOON, THE FLAMES.` → `A BOY WHO WALKED OUT OF THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a demon king, Hiranyakashipu. After years of fierce austerity, he wins an extraordinary protection: he can't be killed by man or beast, by day or by night, indoors or outdoors, on the ground or in the air, by any weapon. Believing himself unkillable, he orders everyone to worship him. Everyone does, except his own small son, Prahlada. Asked what the best thing he's learned is, the boy answers: hearing about Vishnu, singing his names, remembering him. The Bhagavata Purana says his father tries poison, elephants, snakes, a cliff; each time the boy is kept safe. Then comes the part told at Holi bonfires. The king's sister, Holika, is protected against fire. She takes Prahlada onto her lap and sits in a blazing pyre. And the fire goes the other way. Holika burns. Prahlada walks out untouched, still saying the name. Said plainly: the Bhagavata doesn't tell the Holika episode; it lives in other retellings and in the festival itself. Soon after, Vishnu comes as Narasimha, half man, half lion, and ends the king's cruelty. Here's the teaching. Prahlada is bhakti's model devotee, and his answer begins the classic list of ways Hindus love God. Saying the name is the simplest, and the story says it's a refuge no tyrant can take. So the bonfire is Holika Dahan, the burning of Holika. People circle it, as on day one hundred thirty-four, toss in new grain, and call it good's victory over evil.
screen: `A KING WHO THOUGHT HE COULDN'T DIE.` · `A SON WHO WOULDN'T STOP SAYING THE NAME.` · `HOLIKA BURNS; PRAHLADA WALKS OUT.` · `BHAKTI: HEAR, SING, REMEMBER.` · then, large: `HOLIKA DAHAN: THE BONFIRE.`

segments.voice: Picture the bonfire, the heat on your face, the full moon above. Name one thing you'd like to put on it, a grudge, a fear, a habit of cruelty, and watch it burn to ash. Then do what Prahlada did. If you pray, say a name you love, Ram, Krishna, or Om Namo Narayanaya, once with each breath, even with all the noise around you. If you don't, hold one true thing you won't trade away.
Holi. The spring festival that begins the night before, with a bonfire for Prahlada, the boy the fire couldn't burn. Today's word.
Your line: bhakti. Prahlada held the name, and it held him. Tomorrow, the colors come out. That's day one hundred forty-one.

142.title: Holi: the colors of Braj
142.hook: the morning after the fire: Krishna, Radha, a handful of color, and lila, God at play
142.carry: lila: god plays, and love plays back
142.howItsDone: On Holi morning many Hindus greet elders first with a touch of gulal and a bow, then play with colored powder and water with family, friends and neighbors, sharing sweets like gujiya; in Braj, where the colors recall Krishna and Radha, the celebrations run for days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the night before Holi: the bonfire, and Prahlada walking out of the flames. Your line: bhakti. Prahlada held the name, and it held him.

The fire has burned down to ash. Some people carry a little of it home, still warm, and touch it to their foreheads. The next morning, the street belongs to color. Pink, green, yellow, a purple that won't wash out until Thursday. But why color? Nothing in Prahlada's story is pink. For the colors, people tell a different, smaller story, set in a village by a river, about a boy who was worried about his skin. And that story tells you how to play Holi well.
screen: `THE ASH, CARRIED HOME.` → `WHY COLOR?` → `A SECOND, SMALLER STORY.`

segments.voice: The boy is Krishna, growing up among cowherds in Braj, the country around Mathura and Vrindavan. He's dark; the old poems call his skin the color of a rain cloud. The story people tell is that he goes to his foster mother, Yashoda, upset: why is Radha so fair, and I'm so dark? Yashoda laughs: go and put some color on her face, then. So he does, and Radha and her friends put color right back on him. It's a story families and songs tell, not a scene from an old scripture. But it carries one of Hinduism's big ideas: lila, God's play. In Braj, Krishna isn't a distant king. He's the Lord, and he plays: he steals butter, he dances, he throws color. And in Braj devotion, Radha is the greatest of his devotees, so close in love that the color goes both ways. Holi lets everyone join the game. In Barsana, Radha's village in the stories, women playfully chase the men from Krishna's village with long sticks, and the men hide behind shields and laugh. In Vrindavan, some temples throw flower petals instead of powder. Many people read the morning this way: for a few hours, everyone is the same messy color, old and young, boss and worker, and the distance between people drops. So the manners matter. You start with elders: a pinch of gulal, the soft powder, on their feet, and a bow. You say happy Holi first, and you don't color anyone who's said no. God plays, and love plays back.

If you don't, picture someone you've drifted from: say happy Holi first, wait for the smile, a small pinch of pink on their cheek, and let them color you right back.

143.title: The Goddess in all beings
143.hook: a red book read aloud before sunrise for nine mornings, and the hymn at its heart: the Goddess in all beings
143.carry: shakti: the goddess lives in all beings as power
143.tomorrow: Kanya puja: girls as the Goddess
143.howItsDone: During Navaratri many Hindus read or recite the Devi Mahatmya (the Durga Saptashati) across the nine nights and honor the Goddess in nine forms, the Navadurga, one each night, with fasting and prayers; the tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holi in the morning: Krishna, Radha, and a pinch of color. Your line: lila. God plays, and love plays back.
screen: `HOLI: GOD PLAYS, AND LOVE PLAYS BACK.`

segments.voice: Before sunrise, in a small kitchen in Kolkata, a grandmother sits on a low stool with a red cloth-bound book open on her knees. She reads aloud in Sanskrit, fast and steady, the way you read something you've read every autumn of your life. A lamp burns beside her. She'll do this every morning until the ninth. Inside are the battles you heard on day eighty-seven. But today, one hymn from the middle of the book, sung by gods who had lost everything.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE, A RED BOOK.` → `READ ALOUD, NINE MORNINGS.` → `ONE HYMN AT ITS HEART.`

segments.voice: The book is the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess. Many families read it, or have a priest read it, across the nine nights; it also goes by Durga Saptashati, the seven hundred, after its traditional count of verses. It tells three battles, and in the third there's a scene. Two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken heaven. The gods, thrown out, climb into the Himalaya and do the only thing left: they praise the Goddess. Their hymn is one of the most loved in Hinduism. Line after line, they bow to the Goddess who lives in all beings: as consciousness, as sleep, as hunger, as strength, as patience, as faith, as compassion, as mother. And every line ends the same way: we bow to her, we bow to her, again and again. Just then Parvati comes down to bathe in the river. Whom are you praising? she asks. And out of her own body steps another goddess, shining, who answers: they're praising me. Then she goes out to meet the brothers. Here's the teaching under the festival. The Goddess is Shakti, power itself: not only a figure riding a lion, but the strength inside every living thing, even sleep, hunger, a mother's care. That's why the nights are kept for nine forms, the Navadurga, one each night, from Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain, to Siddhidatri, who gives perfection. Many families greet her with Jai Mata Di, victory to the Mother. The same power, nine faces, and the same power in the people in your own house.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA, READ ALOUD.` · `THE GODS' HYMN: IN ALL BEINGS.` · `WE BOW TO HER, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SHAKTI: POWER ITSELF.` · then, large: `THE SAME POWER, NINE FACES.`

segments.voice: Sit with the lamp, the way the grandmother does. If you pray, say Jai Mata Di softly, or the hymn's refrain: we bow to her, again and again. Then think of the strength in one ordinary person near you: a grandmother's patience, a friend's nerve, your own tired body still going. In Navaratri's eyes, that's her. Bow to it inside. If you don't pray, simply notice it, and be grateful for it.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, kept with her book read aloud and one of her nine forms honored each night.
Your line: shakti. The Goddess lives in all beings as power. That's day one hundred forty-three.

144.title: Kanya puja: girls as the Goddess
144.hook: a pot of earth with seeds, a fast, and on the eighth day small girls seated and fed as the Goddess
144.carry: kanya puja: every girl honored as the goddess
144.tomorrow: Janmashtami: the universe in a baby's mouth
144.howItsDone: Many Hindus open Navaratri by setting up a pot as the Goddess's seat and sowing barley beside it, fast on some or all of the nine days, honor young girls as the Goddess in kanya puja on the eighth or ninth day, and keep the nights with garba in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal and golu dolls in the South, ending on Vijayadashami.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri's book: the gods' hymn to the Goddess in all beings. Your line: shakti. The Goddess lives in all beings as power.

It's the first morning of Navaratri in an apartment in Delhi. Before breakfast, someone spreads a layer of soil in a shallow tray and scatters barley over it. In the middle goes a clay pot of water, mango leaves tucked around its neck, a coconut on top. A lamp is lit beside it. Then everyone leaves for work and school. There's nothing to see yet, just a pot and some dirt. But by the ninth day, that tray will be a small field of green.
screen: `FIRST MORNING: SOIL AND SEEDS.` → `A POT, MANGO LEAVES, A COCONUT.` → `BY THE NINTH DAY: GREEN.`

segments.voice: Start at the end of the Goddess's book. The last demon king has fallen, and the gods, saved, sing her one more hymn of thanks. In it they say something families still act out: every kind of knowledge is a form of you, Goddess, and so is every woman in the world. And she answers with a promise: whenever trouble rises, call me, and I'll come again. Navaratri is that calling. It opens with ghatasthapana. Ghata, the pot. Sthapana, setting it up. Many families invite the Goddess to be present in that pot for the nine days, and sow barley beside it, jau in Hindi. Many fast, some until evening, many by setting grain aside for buckwheat, fruit and milk. Then, on the eighth or ninth day, comes the custom that surprises people most. Families invite young girls from the neighborhood into the house. They wash the girls' feet, mark their foreheads, seat them like honored guests and feed them, often puri, chickpeas and a sweet halwa, with a small gift at the end. It's called kanya puja, and the girls are honored as forms of the Goddess herself. That's the teaching, said plainly. The Goddess isn't only in the pot or on the shrine. Her power is honored in living girls and women, the ones at your own table. Many teachers draw the harder lesson too: a girl worshiped on the eighth night can't be treated as less on any other day. On the tenth day comes Vijayadashami, the victory, and in some homes the green shoots are handed out as a blessing.

145.howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, sing and retell Krishna's birth in homes and temples, and at midnight bathe an image of baby Krishna in panchamrita, dress him, and rock him in a cradle before breaking the fast; many homes care for a baby Krishna image all year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri as it's kept: a pot, sprouting barley, and little girls honored as the Goddess. Your line: kanya puja. Every girl honored as the Goddess.

It's eleven forty-five at night, and nobody in the house is asleep. Grandma hasn't eaten since morning. In the corner is a tiny wooden cradle hung with flowers, and in it a little image of a baby. The temple down the road is packed, singing the same few lines louder as the minutes pass. At midnight, the conch shells blow and everyone shouts. This is Janmashtami, Krishna's birth. You've heard the night he was born. Today, a story about the baby, and why a house rocks a cradle for God.
screen: `ELEVEN FORTY-FIVE. NOBODY'S ASLEEP.` → `A CRADLE WITH FLOWERS.` → `AT MIDNIGHT, THE CONCH.`

segments.voice: Krishna, born at midnight in a king's prison, was carried across the river and raised in Gokul by Yashoda, the cowherd woman who loved him as her own. One day the other children run to her: Krishna's been eating dirt! Yashoda grabs him. Open your mouth. He says he didn't do it; they're telling tales. Open it, she says. He opens it. And inside that little mouth she sees everything: the sky and the stars, the earth with its mountains and oceans, fire and wind, time itself, and her own village, and herself, standing there, looking into his mouth. She's terrified. Is this a dream? Then, the story says, Krishna lets the vision fade, and she forgets it. She just sets him on her lap, her boy again. That's from the Bhagavata Purana, and it holds the teaching under Janmashtami. Hindus call this kind of love vatsalya, a parent's tender love, offered to God. The God who holds the universe lets himself be loved like a baby: fed, bathed, scolded, rocked to sleep. Many teachers say Yashoda's love is sweeter to God than all the awe in the world. So on Janmashtami, families don't only bow. Many fast and stay awake singing until midnight, the hour he was born. Then baby Krishna is bathed like a newborn in panchamrita, the five nectars: milk, yogurt, honey, ghee and sugar. He's dressed in new clothes and laid in the cradle, and people take turns giving it a push. The infinite God, small enough to hold.

146.title: Ganapati comes to the street
146.hook: a clay Ganesha carried home under a cloth, and how the god every Hindu begins with went out into the street
146.carry: ganapati: lord of the ganas, first for everyone
146.howItsDone: On Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindus bring a clay image of Ganesha home or to a neighborhood pavilion, invite his presence with prana pratishtha, and honor him daily with flowers, durva grass, modak and arti for one and a half to ten days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janmashtami: a fast, a cradle, and the universe in a baby's mouth. Your line: vatsalya. Loving the infinite God as a child.
screen: `JANMASHTAMI: THE INFINITE, SMALL ENOUGH TO HOLD.`

segments.voice: In Maharashtra, in late summer, you'll see a family walking home from the market carrying a Ganesha about the size of a toddler, his face covered with a cloth. A cousin is banging a drum. The kids are shouting Ganpati Bappa Morya. He's made of clay, still slightly damp. At home, a corner has been cleared, a little platform set up, flowers ready. They'll uncover his face only once he's in his seat. Down the road, a whole neighborhood is putting up a pavilion for a Ganesha three times as tall. Today, the arrival.
screen: `A CLAY GANESHA, FACE COVERED.` → `GANPATI BAPPA MORYA.` → `A GUEST FOR A FEW DAYS.`

segments.voice: Chaturthi means the fourth day, the fourth of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September, the day Ganesha is said to have been born. Remember day twenty-four: Shiva gives the boy an elephant's head, makes him leader of the ganas, his band of followers, and promises he'll be worshipped first. That's his name. Gana-pati: lord of the ganas, the hosts, the crowd. And the promise holds in a way few gods share: Hindus of almost every tradition, whether they mainly love Shiva, Vishnu or the Goddess, begin with Ganesha. Now a story from history. For a long time Ganesh Chaturthi was kept mostly at home. Then in 1893, in Pune, the freedom fighter Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn it into a great public festival. Ganeshas went up in the street, in pavilions put up by whole neighborhoods, with music and speeches, and people came from every lane of the city, under British rule, to gather around a god they all shared. At home, the image is invited in with prana pratishtha, setting the breath in, and from then on he's treated as present: flowers, blades of durva grass, modak, the sweet dumplings in his hand, and arti morning and evening. Here's the teaching. Ganapati is the god of the crowd: the one every Hindu home begins with, and so the one a whole street can welcome together. And like any guest, he only stays a while. Tomorrow, the leaving.
screen: `CHATURTHI, THE FOURTH DAY.` · `GANAPATI: LORD OF THE GANAS.` · `1893: THE FESTIVAL GOES PUBLIC.` · `INVITED IN, AND TREATED AS PRESENT.` · then, large: `FIRST FOR EVERYONE.`

147.title: Visarjan: the god who stays
147.hook: Ganesha carried to the water, a boy's pillar remembered, and why nothing is lost when the clay goes under
147.carry: visarjan: god stays when the clay goes
147.howItsDone: At the end of Ganesh Chaturthi, after one and a half to ten days, many Hindus perform a final arti and carry the clay Ganesha in procession to a river, lake or the sea for visarjan, chanting Ganpati Bappa Morya; many now use plain clay or immerse at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi: Ganesha welcomed home and into the street. Your line was Ganapati, lord of the ganas, first for everyone.

It's the last day. The Ganesha who's been sitting in the living room, fed and sung to, is lifted off his seat for one last arti. Then out the door, into a street that's become a river of people: drums, dancing, Ganesha after Ganesha moving slowly toward the sea. At the shore, people wade in and lower him into the water. He slips under. And the whole beach shouts: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Father Ganesha, come early next year. A lot of people are crying.
screen: `ONE LAST ARTI.` → `A RIVER OF PEOPLE TO THE SEA.` → `COME EARLY NEXT YEAR.`

segments.voice: The immersion is called visarjan, from a Sanskrit root meaning to let go, to release. It happens on different days in different homes: after a day and a half, or three, five, seven, and the biggest crowds on Anant Chaturdashi, ten days after Chaturthi. So why make a god from clay, feed him for days, and then give him to the water? Go back to the start of the week, to Prahlada. His furious father points at a stone pillar. Your Vishnu is everywhere, you say? Is he in this pillar? Yes, says the boy. The king strikes it, and out of the stone bursts Narasimha. That's the teaching under visarjan, the way many Hindus explain it: God is everywhere already. The clay image was a seat where he was invited to sit for a while, never the whole of him. Every puja has these two moments, the inviting, avahana, and the sending off, visarjana; Ganesh Chaturthi just makes them as big as a city. So nothing is lost when the clay goes under: it goes home to the water. Many families close with a short prayer that says, roughly: I don't know how to call you, or how to send you off; forgive whatever I did wrong. One modern problem: plaster images don't dissolve, so many families have gone back to plain clay, some immersing at home in a bucket. And look back at the week: a boy in the fire, colors in Braj, the Mother in every being, a baby holding the universe, Ganapati in the street. Five ways of loving God, kept with your hands.
screen: `VISARJAN: TO LET GO.` · `IS HE IN THIS PILLAR?` · `INVITED IN, SENT OFF: EVERY PUJA.` · `THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE WATER.` · then, large: `GOD STAYS WHEN THE CLAY GOES.`

segments.voice: Picture yesterday's Ganesha. One last arti, the lamp circling his face. Carry him with the drums to the water's edge, lower him gently, and let go; watch the water close. If you pray, say the closing prayer in your own words: I didn't know how to call you or send you off; forgive what I got wrong; come again. If you don't, say it to the year that's ending: thank you, come again.
Ganesh Chaturthi. He arrives in clay on the fourth day, stays as a guest, and is given back to the water, with a promise to come again.
Your line: visarjan. God stays when the clay goes. That's the week, and day one hundred forty-seven.
